questions.prompt: All are the following are examples of Non-Specific response Except
options: sensitized T lymphocytes or B Lymphocytes
questions.suggestedLabel: B. sensitized T lymphocytes or B Lymphocytes
questions.suggestedRationale: Sensitized T and B lymphocytes are specific (adaptive) immunity; the others are nonspecific defenses.

questions.prompt: The inflammatory response is a nonspecific response to
questions.suggestedRationale: Inflammation is a nonspecific response to any tissue injury.

questions.prompt: Example of Chemical Mediators are:
Edema associated with inflammation results from
options: increased fluid and protein in the interstitial compartment.
increased phagocytes in the affected area.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. increased fluid and protein in the interstitial compartment.
questions.suggestedRationale: Inflammatory edema comes from leaky capillaries that put fluid and protein into the interstitium.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the following events in the inflammatory response immediately after tissue injury?
options: Migration of leukocytes to the area
questions.suggestedRationale: After injury: brief vasoconstriction, then dilation and hyperemia, increased permeability, and leukocyte migration.

questions.prompt: Mechanisms to bring an elevated body temperature down to the normal level include
questions.suggestedRationale: Cutaneous vasodilation sheds heat; shivering and higher metabolic rate would raise temperature.

questions.prompt: Which of the following spices does NOT show anti-inflammatory action?
questions.suggestedRationale: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is not a spice and has little anti-inflammatory effect, unlike turmeric, ginger, or basil.

questions.prompt: Cytokines are chemical mediators released by
questions.suggestedRationale: Cytokines are produced especially by macrophages (and T cells); that is the best match among the options.

questions.prompt: A substance normally not found in the blood, but appears with acute inflammation and necrosis within 24 to 48 hours is
questions.suggestedRationale: C-reactive protein appears in serum within 24–48 hours of acute inflammation or necrosis.

questions.prompt: Hypermetabolism is common with major burns because of
options: increased heat loss from the burn wound.
questions.suggestedRationale: Major burns raise metabolic demand through heat loss, tissue repair, and an ongoing stress response.

questions.prompt: Emergency care for burn involves which of the following
options: Drop and lie completely still on your back.
Call a neighbor for help if the burn appears to be extensive.
Apply lotion and cover burn tightly with a sheet or towel.
Cover the burn area with clean, cool, or tepid water and remove nonsticking clothing
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Cover the burn area with clean, cool, or tepid water and remove nonsticking clothing
questions.suggestedRationale: Cool the burn with clean tepid water and remove clothing that is not stuck to the wound.

questions.prompt: Severity of Burn is related to:
options: Burn depends on the temperature, duration, and extent of the burn.
The age of the person, children are prone to severe burns more than adults or elderely
Burns are dependent on the location of the body.
With a major burn, excessive bleeding usually causes shock.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Burn depends on the temperature, duration, and extent of the burn.
questions.suggestedRationale: Burn severity depends mainly on temperature, duration, and extent of the burn (the option even flags this as correct).

questions.prompt: Identify the proper sequence in the healing process.
options: A blood clot forms; granulation tissue grows into the gap; new blood vessels develop; phagocytosis of foreign material and cell debris occurs; and collagen fibers form a tight, strong scar.
A blood clot forms; phagocytes remove foreign material and cell debris; granulation tissue grows into the gap; new blood vessels form; and collagen fibers promote formation of a tight, strong scar.
Collagen fibers form in the damaged area; a blood clot forms; granulation tissue grows into the gap; angiogenesis takes place; and foreign material and cell debris are removed by phagocytes.
Foreign material and cell debris are removed by phagocytes; a blood clot forms; granulation tissue grows into the gap; new blood vessels form; and collagen fibers grow and cross-link.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. A blood clot forms; phagocytes remove foreign material and cell debris; granulation tissue grows into the gap; new blood vessels form; and collagen fibers promote formation of a tight, strong scar.
questions.suggestedRationale: Healing sequence: clot, phagocytic cleanup, granulation tissue and new vessels, then collagen scar.

questions.prompt: Why is an application of cold recommended as part of the RICE first aid measures immediately following an inflammatory response due to injury?
options: It improves circulation in the area removing chemical mediators.
It causes local vasoconstriction to reduce local edema.
It draws more phagocytic cells to the area to remove debris.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. It causes local vasoconstriction to reduce local edema.
questions.suggestedRationale: Cold causes local vasoconstriction, which limits swelling after injury (RICE).

questions.prompt: Which of the following cellular elements found in the inflammatory response are responsible for phagocytosis?
questions.suggestedRationale: Macrophages are the main phagocytic cells listed; lymphocytes are not professional phagocytes.

questions.prompt: Drugs that have anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic activities include
questions.suggestedRationale: NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors, ibuprofen, and aspirin are anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic; acetaminophen is not anti-inflammatory, and steroids are not NSAID-type analgesics.

questions.prompt: Causes of inflammation include
options: direct physical damage such as cuts and sprains.
questions.suggestedRationale: Physical injury, allergy, and infection can all trigger inflammation.

questions.prompt: Nonspecific agents that protect uninfected cells against viruses are called
questions.suggestedRationale: Interferons protect nearby uninfected cells from viruses.

questions.prompt: An abscess contains
questions.suggestedRationale: An abscess is a pocket of purulent (pus) exudate.

questions.prompt: What increases in blood to promote phagocytosis
options: nothing changes its part of natural defense mechanism
questions.suggestedRationale: Neutrophils rise in the blood and carry out acute phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: Healing of large areas of skin loss (including dermis and epidermis) would be most successful through
options: rapid mitosis and regeneration of skin layers.
resolution of damaged cells in the area.
covering the area with biosynthetic skin substitute.
graft of fibrous tissue to the area.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. covering the area with biosynthetic skin substitute.
questions.suggestedRationale: Full-thickness skin loss heals best when covered with a graft or biosynthetic substitute, not by simple regeneration.

questions.prompt: How does Ice help with reducing edema to any injured site?
options: ICE reduces pain to reduce swelling
questions.suggestedRationale: Ice reduces edema by local vasoconstriction.

questions.prompt: Prolonged administration of glucocorticoids such as prednisone may cause
questions.suggestedRationale: Long-term glucocorticoids atrophy lymphoid tissue and decrease protein synthesis (and actually lower, not raise, infection resistance).

questions.prompt: A serous exudate is best described as a
questions.suggestedRationale: Serous exudate is thin, watery, and relatively clear or colorless.

questions.prompt: The advantages of applying a biosynthetic skin substitute to a large area of full-thickness burns include
options: decreased loss of plasma protein and fluid.
regeneration of all glands, nerves, and hair follicles.
questions.suggestedRationale: Skin substitutes reduce infection and protein/fluid loss and speed coverage; full-thickness burns do not regenerate glands, nerves, or hair.

questions.prompt: The presence of the bacterial capsule
options: aids in the release of endotoxins.
increases the release of toxins and enzymes.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. protects the microbe from phagocytosis.
questions.suggestedRationale: A capsule helps bacteria evade phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: Microbial mutation means that
options: the microbe survives adverse conditions but can no longer replicate.
the immune response to that microbe is strengthened.
questions.suggestedRationale: Mutation means the organism’s genetic information has changed.

questions.prompt: A bacterial endospore can
options: also be classified as an acid-fast bacterium.
exist in latent form inside a host cell.
survive high temperatures and a dry environment.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. survive high temperatures and a dry environment.
questions.suggestedRationale: Endospores can survive heat and drying.

questions.prompt: The structure of a virus includes
options: a protein coat and either DNA or RNA.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. a protein coat and either DNA or RNA.
questions.suggestedRationale: A virus has a protein capsid and a DNA or RNA genome, not a true cell wall or its own metabolic enzymes.

questions.prompt: A retrovirus such as HIV contains
options: RNA and enzymes for its conversion.
many enzymes to limit budding of new virions.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. RNA and enzymes for its conversion.
questions.suggestedRationale: HIV is a retrovirus: RNA plus reverse transcriptase to convert it to DNA.

questions.prompt: How do antiviral drugs act?
options: They interfere with cell wall development.
They destroy new, immature viral particles.
They reduce the rate of viral replication.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. They reduce the rate of viral replication.
questions.suggestedRationale: Antiviral drugs slow viral replication; they do not typically destroy every virion or attack bacterial cell walls.

questions.prompt: What is true for Fungi
questions.suggestedRationale: Fungi reproduce by budding, hyphal extension, and spores, not by binary fission.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT classified as a protozoan agent of disease?
questions.suggestedRationale: Tinea pedis is a fungus (dermatophyte), not a protozoan.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic of rickettsia?
options: It is a very small gram-negative intracellular microbe
questions.suggestedLabel: A. It is a very small gram-negative intracellular microbe
questions.suggestedRationale: Rickettsiae are tiny gram-negative obligate intracellular bacteria.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is normally considered sterile?
questions.suggestedRationale: Urine in the bladder is normally sterile; the pharynx, sputum, and urethra carry flora.

questions.prompt: WHat is a nosocomial infection?
options: transmission involves an insect or animal host.
acquired in a hospital or medical facility.
spread by direct contact with secretions from an open lesion.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. acquired in a hospital or medical facility.
questions.suggestedRationale: A nosocomial infection is acquired in a hospital or other health-care facility.

questions.prompt: Which of the following factors would NOT increase the virulence of a specific microbe?
questions.suggestedRationale: Interferons are a host defense, not a microbial virulence factor.

questions.prompt: That time in the course of an infection when the infected person may experience a headache or fatigue and senses he or she is “coming down with something” is referred to as which of the following?
questions.suggestedRationale: The prodromal period is the early 'coming down with something' phase (headache, fatigue).

questions.prompt: The principle of Universal Precautions is based on
options: using disinfectants at all times to eliminate cross-infections.
not touching any open or bleeding lesions.
sterilizing all instruments and equipment after each use.
assuming that all body fluids from all individuals are possible sources of infection.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. assuming that all body fluids from all individuals are possible sources of infection.
questions.suggestedRationale: Standard/universal precautions assume every person’s body fluids may be infectious.

questions.prompt: What does “bacteremia” refer to?
options: Numerous pathogens circulating and reproducing in the blood
Multiple infections, primary and secondary, established in the body
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Microbes present in the blood
questions.suggestedRationale: Bacteremia means bacteria are present in the blood; option A describes septicemia (replicating pathogens in the bloodstream).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a local sign of infection?
questions.suggestedRationale: Pain, redness, and swelling are local signs; fever and leukocytosis are systemic.

questions.prompt: What are culture and sensitivity tests used for?
options: To determine the type of microbe present in an exudate
To provide a specific medium that supports maximum microbial growth
To identify the causative microbe and the effective antimicrobial agent for it
To provide living host cells for microbes requiring such for replication
questions.suggestedLabel: C. To identify the causative microbe and the effective antimicrobial agent for it
questions.suggestedRationale: Culture and sensitivity identify the organism and which drug will work.

questions.prompt: A broad-spectrum bactericidal agent would be expected to
options: destroy many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
destroy all pathogenic microbes in contact with the agent.
reduce the replication of many bacteria.
inhibit the growth of most spores and acid-fast bacteria.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. destroy many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
questions.suggestedRationale: A broad-spectrum bactericidal drug kills many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

questions.prompt: What does “bacteremia” refer to?
options: Numerous pathogens circulating and reproducing in the blood
Multiple infections, primary and secondary, established in the body
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Microbes present in the blood
questions.suggestedRationale: Same distinction as earlier: bacteremia is presence of microbes in blood, not uncontrolled sepsis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a local sign of infection?
questions.suggestedRationale: Local infection signs are pain, erythema, and swelling.

questions.prompt: Secondary infection may occur with administration of antibacterial drugs because the
options: patient is allergic to the drug.
balance of species in the resident flora is upset.
mucosa of the stomach is irritated.
infecting microbes spread to adjacent areas.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. balance of species in the resident flora is upset.
questions.suggestedRationale: Antibacterials can wipe out normal flora and allow a secondary (often opportunistic) infection.

questions.prompt: All of the following are mechanisms of antiviral drug action EXCEPT
options: interference with attachment to host cell.
questions.suggestedRationale: Viruses do not undergo mitosis, so blocking mitosis is not an antiviral mechanism.

questions.prompt: Secondary bacterial infections occur frequently during influenza epidemics primarily because
options: the virus causes extensive tissue inflammation and necrosis.
the viral infection is usually self-limiting.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. the virus causes extensive tissue inflammation and necrosis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Influenza necroses respiratory mucosa, opening the way for secondary bacterial infection.

questions.prompt: What does leukocytosis frequently indicate?
options: Presence of a specific bacterial infection
questions.suggestedRationale: Leukocytosis commonly indicates a bacterial infection.

questions.prompt: When an infection or inflammation is suspected, what does leucopenia often indicate?
questions.suggestedRationale: Viral infections more often cause leukopenia than bacterial infections do.

questions.prompt: The widespread necrosis of respiratory mucosa caused by an influenza infection often gives rise to
questions.suggestedRationale: Necrotic respiratory mucosa after influenza commonly leads to secondary infection.

questions.prompt: Prions cannot be cultured in a PETRI plate of media because
options: they take so long to grow.
they require extensive amounts of specialized nutrients.
they are proteinaceous particles, not living organisms.
they are viruses that don’t grow on conventional media.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. they are proteinaceous particles, not living organisms.
questions.suggestedRationale: Prions are infectious proteins, not organisms that grow on culture media.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does NOT directly determine the virulence of a microbe?
questions.suggestedRationale: Opportunism depends mainly on host defenses; toxins, invasiveness, and mutation more directly define virulence.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the primary difference between an antiseptic and a disinfectant?
options: Antiseptic is used on living tissue, whereas disinfectant is designed for nonliving surfaces
Antiseptic is much stronger than the potency of a disinfectant.
Antiseptic often causes allergic skin reactions, whereas disinfectant is always hypoallergenic.
Antiseptic is effective against endospores; disinfectants are not effective against endospores.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Antiseptic is used on living tissue, whereas disinfectant is designed for nonliving surfaces
questions.suggestedRationale: Antiseptics are for living tissue; disinfectants are for inanimate surfaces.

questions.prompt: What are Neutrophils?
options: are elevated during an allergic response.
questions.suggestedRationale: Neutrophils are phagocytes.

questions.prompt: Humoral immunity is mediated by
questions.suggestedRationale: Humoral immunity is mediated by B lymphocytes and their antibodies.

questions.prompt: A secondary immune response differs from the primary immune response in that
options: it is more rapid than the primary response and results in higher antibody levels
it is slower than the primary response and doesn’t change the antibody levels.
it occurs at the same time as the primary response but results in a decrease in antibodies.
it only occurs in hyperallergic reactions and results in a decrease of antibodies.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. it is more rapid than the primary response and results in higher antibody levels
questions.suggestedRationale: A secondary (anamnestic) response is faster and produces higher antibody titers.

questions.prompt: Which type of immunity is provided by a vaccination?
questions.suggestedRationale: Vaccination is active artificial immunity.

questions.prompt: Which cells are required to process and present antigens from foreign material as the initial step in the immune response?
questions.suggestedRationale: Macrophages process and present antigen as the usual first step in the adaptive response.

questions.prompt: When an allergen binds with IgE antibodies on mast cells, resulting in release of chemical mediators, this reaction is called
questions.suggestedRationale: IgE on mast cells plus allergen is type I hypersensitivity.

questions.prompt: The role of memory cells is to
options: change into an antibody-secreting cell following activation.
immediately secrete antibodies following the first exposure to antigen.
recognize the antigen and stimulate the immune response
questions.suggestedLabel: C. recognize the antigen and stimulate the immune response
questions.suggestedRationale: Memory cells recognize re-exposure and quickly restart a strong immune response.

questions.prompt: Which statement applies to contact dermatitis?
options: It occurs when IgE antibodies on the skin react with the causative substance.
It may result from ingested foods.
Urticaria (hives) gradually spread over the body.
A type IV reaction occurs in affected areas
questions.suggestedLabel: D. A type IV reaction occurs in affected areas
questions.suggestedRationale: Contact dermatitis is a type IV (delayed, cell-mediated) reaction in the exposed skin.

questions.prompt: Which of the following causes anaphylaxis?
options: Immune complex deposits in many tissue
questions.suggestedLabel: A. A severe, systemic allergic reaction
questions.suggestedRationale: Anaphylaxis is a severe systemic type I allergic reaction.

questions.prompt: Following a positive HIV antibodies blood test and ELISA test, what is the test commonly used for confirmation?
questions.suggestedRationale: Western blot is the classic confirmatory test after a positive HIV ELISA.

questions.prompt: Systemic lupus erythematosus is caused by
options: immune complex deposits of antinuclear antibodies.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. immune complex deposits of antinuclear antibodies.
questions.suggestedRationale: SLE involves immune-complex deposits of antinuclear antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are the target cells for HIV?
questions.suggestedRationale: HIV primarily infects CD4 helper T lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: A diagnosis of HIV positive means that
options: the number of T lymphocytes in the circulating blood is decreased.
significant opportunistic infection is present in the body.
the virus and its antibodies are present in the blood.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. the virus and its antibodies are present in the blood.
questions.suggestedRationale: HIV-positive means virus and antibodies are in the blood; it is not the same as a diagnosis of AIDS.

questions.prompt: Serious infections frequently occurring in patients with AIDS include
questions.suggestedRationale: TB and Pneumocystis pneumonia are the classic serious opportunistic infections in AIDS.

questions.prompt: Host-versus-graft disease refers to
options: T cells in grafted tissue attacking host cells.
transplant rejection by the recipient’s immune system
questions.suggestedLabel: D. transplant rejection by the recipient’s immune system
questions.suggestedRationale: Host-versus-graft disease is rejection of the transplant by the recipient’s immune system (the reverse of GVHD).

questions.prompt: Which of the following characteristics apply to HIV?
options: It contains two strands of DNA.
It tends to mutate frequently to form new strains.
The incubation period is extremely short.
It is inactivated by heat and many disinfectants.
questions.suggestedRationale: HIV is an RNA virus that mutates often and is inactivated by heat and many disinfectants; the latent period is long, not extremely short.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an effect of cytokines? They
options: activate and stimulate proliferation of B and T lymphocytes.
increase the rate of mitosis in tumors.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. activate and stimulate proliferation of B and T lymphocytes.
questions.suggestedRationale: Cytokines activate and expand B and T lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding a patient who is HIV positive?
options: No medication is required until the CD4 cell count drops below normal range.
Antibodies are present, destroying the virus and preventing transmission to others.
Antibodies in the blood indicate presence of virus and possible transmission to others.
Enzymes have not yet converted RNA to DNA for replication.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Antibodies in the blood indicate presence of virus and possible transmission to others.
questions.suggestedRationale: HIV antibodies mean the virus is present and the person can transmit it; they do not clear the infection.

questions.prompt: The most common cause of death in patients who have AIDS is
questions.suggestedRationale: Standard patho texts list Pneumocystis pneumonia as the most common cause of death in AIDS.

questions.prompt: The most common clinical condition associated with a cytokine storm is
questions.suggestedRationale: A cytokine storm is classically associated with acute respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.prompt: Which of the following areas lacks blood vessels and nerves?
questions.suggestedRationale: The epidermis has no blood vessels or nerves.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a common effect of a type I hypersensitivity response to ingested substances?
questions.suggestedRationale: Type I reactions to ingested allergens commonly produce urticaria (hives).

questions.prompt: What change occurs in the skin with psoriasis?
options: Increased mitosis and shedding of epithelium
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Increased mitosis and shedding of epithelium
questions.suggestedRationale: Psoriasis shows rapid keratinocyte turnover and shedding of silvery scale.

questions.prompt: Why do secondary infections frequently develop in pruritic lesions?
options: Entry of resident flora while scratching the lesion
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Entry of resident flora while scratching the lesion
questions.suggestedRationale: Scratching pruritic lesions lets resident flora enter and cause secondary infection.

questions.prompt: Which of the following skin lesions are usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.suggestedRationale: Furuncles (boils) are usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.prompt: What is the common signal that a recurrence of herpes simplex infection is developing?
options: Mild tingling along the nerve or on the lips
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Mild tingling along the nerve or on the lips
questions.suggestedRationale: Recurrent herpes simplex is often heralded by mild tingling along the nerve or on the lips.

questions.prompt: How are antiviral drugs effective in treating a viral infection?
options: They destroy the virus if administered for at least 2 weeks.
They limit the acute stage and viral shedding.
They prevent any systemic effects of viruses.
They prevent any secondary bacterial infection.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. They limit the acute stage and viral shedding.
questions.suggestedRationale: Antivirals shorten the acute phase and reduce viral shedding; they do not eradicate the virus.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements regarding acute necrotizing fasciitis is TRUE?
options: Infection is localized in a small area of the epidermis.
It is usually caused by S. aureus.
Spontaneous recovery usually occurs in 48 hours.
Infection rapidly causes extensive tissue necrosis and toxic shock
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Infection rapidly causes extensive tissue necrosis and toxic shock
questions.suggestedRationale: Necrotizing fasciitis spreads rapidly with extensive necrosis and can cause toxic shock.

questions.prompt: Which type of microbe causes Tinea infections?
questions.suggestedRationale: Tinea infections are caused by dermatophyte fungi.

questions.prompt: How can pediculosis be diagnosed?
options: Pruritus in hairy areas of the body
Loss of blood due to lice bites
The presence of nits at the base of hair shafts
questions.suggestedLabel: D. The presence of nits at the base of hair shafts
questions.suggestedRationale: Pediculosis is confirmed by finding nits attached at the base of hair shafts.

questions.prompt: All of the following statements apply to malignant melanoma EXCEPT:
options: The malignant cell is a melanocyte.
They present as non-pruritic purplish macules.
The neoplasm grows rapidly and metastasizes early.
The lesion is usually dark or multicolored with an irregular border.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. They present as non-pruritic purplish macules.
questions.suggestedRationale: Melanoma is not a non-pruritic purplish macule (that description fits Kaposi sarcoma better).

questions.prompt: Which of the following factors has contributed to the increased incidence of Kaposi’s sarcoma?
questions.suggestedRationale: Kaposi sarcoma incidence rose with the number of immunosuppressed patients (especially AIDS).

questions.prompt: The cause of contact dermatitis can often be identified by
options: using a culture and sensitivity test on the exudate.
checking the frequency of the exacerbations.
noting the location and size of the lesion.
the type of pain associated with the lesion
questions.suggestedLabel: C. noting the location and size of the lesion.
questions.suggestedRationale: The distribution and shape of the rash often identify the contact allergen.

questions.prompt: The pathological change associated with scleroderma is
options: abnormal activation of T lymphocytes and an increase of cytokines.
an autoimmune reaction damaging the epidermis.
collagen deposits in the small blood vessels of the skin and sometimes the viscera.
Type I hypersensitivity and increased serum IgE level
questions.suggestedLabel: C. collagen deposits in the small blood vessels of the skin and sometimes the viscera.
questions.suggestedRationale: Scleroderma deposits collagen in small vessels of the skin and sometimes internal organs.

questions.prompt: Choose the best description of the typical lesion of impetigo.
options: Large, red, painful nodule filled with purulent exudates
Small vesicles that rupture to produce a crusty brown pruritic mass
Red, swollen, painful areas often with projecting red streaks
Firm, raised papules that may have a rough surface and may be painful
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Small vesicles that rupture to produce a crusty brown pruritic mass
questions.suggestedRationale: Impetigo starts as small vesicles that rupture into honey-colored crusts.

questions.prompt: Dupuytren’s contracture is a deformity that involves
options: knots of tissue in the palm of the hand resulting in bent fingers.
tissue atrophy of the long leg muscles.
involuntary contraction of the muscles of the spine.
scar tissue that causes excessive joint pain.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. knots of tissue in the palm of the hand resulting in bent fingers.
questions.suggestedRationale: Dupuytren contracture is palmar fascia thickening that pulls the fingers into flexion.

questions.prompt: One factor that is responsible for increasing the mortality rate among patients suffering with necrotizing fasciitis is
options: the appearance of additional opportunistic infections.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. a delay in initial diagnosis.
questions.suggestedRationale: Delayed diagnosis is a major reason necrotizing fasciitis has a high mortality.
